# TotalFusion: the documentation in one file

> TotalFusion extends Total.js 5 with other runtimes: functions written in Python, Rust, Go and WebAssembly are called from Node.js and Total.js as `async` functions, and become actions, API routes, MCP tools for AI agents, Server-Sent Events and nodes of Flow. Each runtime is a pool of worker processes that Node.js supervises; a crash in a worker never takes the application down. A WebAssembly module runs in a sandbox: no files, no network, no environment.

Node.js 20 or newer, no dependencies, plain JavaScript (no TypeScript). Version 0.1.0, not on npm yet: install it from a clone with `npm install ../totalfusion`. The engine (`require('totalfusion')`) does not depend on Total.js; `fusion.register()`, `fusion.sse()` and `fusion.flow()` do. Nothing is downloaded, compiled or installed for the user. MIT license.

---

# TotalFusion

<p align="center">
  <a href="docs/python.md"><img src="docs/assets/python.svg" alt="Python" height="56"></a>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
  <a href="docs/rust.md"><img src="docs/assets/rust.svg" alt="Rust" height="56"></a>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
  <a href="docs/go.md"><img src="docs/assets/go.svg" alt="Go" height="56"></a>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
  <a href="docs/webassembly.md"><img src="docs/assets/webassembly.svg" alt="WebAssembly" height="56"></a>
</p>

<p align="center"><sub>Python, Rust, Go and WebAssembly &middot; for Total.js and Node.js</sub></p>

<p align="center"><a href="https://github.com/totaljs-es/totalfusion/actions/workflows/test.yml"><img src="https://github.com/totaljs-es/totalfusion/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg" alt="Tests on Linux, macOS and Windows"></a></p>

**Extends Total.js with other runtimes.** Call functions written in Python, Rust and Go from Total.js and Node.js as plain `async` functions, and use them as Actions, API endpoints and MCP tools for AI agents, without leaving JavaScript. WebAssembly modules run in a sandbox.

```python
# python/sentiment.py
from totalfusion import action

@action(summary='Detects the sentiment of a text', input='*text:String', output='label:String', mcp=True)
def analyze(data):
    return { 'label': 'POSITIVE' if 'love' in data['text'] else 'NEGATIVE' }
```

```js
// Total.js application
const fusion = REQUIRE('totalfusion');

fusion.register({ python: { path: PATH.root('python') } });

// 'sentiment/analyze' is now a Total.js action: ACTION(), API routes and an MCP tool for AI agents
const result = await ACTION('sentiment/analyze', { text: 'I love it' }).promise();
```

Total.js validates the input against the contract before Python runs. The engine (`require('totalfusion')`) is plain Node.js and does not depend on Total.js, so `fusion.python('sentiment.analyze', data)` also works in any Node.js program.

## What you get

- **Python, Rust and Go workers** that Node.js supervises: a pool of long-lived processes, correlated calls, timeouts, cancellation and real errors (with the traceback in Python). A crash in a worker never takes your application down. → [Python](docs/python.md), [Rust](docs/rust.md), [Go](docs/go.md)
- **A sandbox**: a WebAssembly module runs without files, network or environment, in one file that works on any system. → [WebAssembly](docs/webassembly.md)
- **Total.js integration**: the functions that declare a contract become actions with validated `input`, `query` and `params`, permissions, API routes, MCP tools, and Server-Sent Events. → [Total.js 5](docs/total5.md)
- **Seven components for Flow**: call a function of any runtime from a node, stream chunks as messages, send the events of the workers to an alert and read the stats. They were run in the designer of Flow. → [Flow](docs/flow.md)
- **Binary data without base64**: `Buffer` and typed arrays travel as raw bytes in both directions, NumPy arrays included. A 100 MB buffer makes the round trip in 43 ms. → [Binary data](docs/binary-data.md)
- **Streaming** with backpressure and cancellation: a generator in Python or a stream function in Rust or Go is an async iterable. → [Streaming](docs/streaming.md)
- **Several calls at once** in one worker, for calls that wait, and for the threads of a Rust worker or the goroutines of a Go one. → [Working with the workers](docs/workers.md)
- **Workers that stay healthy**: replaced after a number of calls or when they use too much memory, with no call lost, and checked while idle. Events for your logs. Optional retry of calls that you declare idempotent. → [Working with the workers](docs/workers.md)
- **Development reload**: save a file and the next call runs the new code. → [Development](docs/development.md)
- **A `doctor`** that tells you what is missing, and the exact command to fix it, before anything runs. → [Development](docs/development.md#checking-your-setup)

## Runtimes

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| [Python](docs/python.md) | Available | Machine learning, scientific computing, any Python library. Python 3.9 or newer. |
| [Rust](docs/rust.md) | Available | Speed, many threads, a small footprint. You build a binary; running it does not need Rust. |
| [WebAssembly](docs/webassembly.md) | Available | Code in a sandbox, in one `.wasm` file for every system. Go is the language with an SDK today. |
| [Go](docs/go.md) | Available | Network and infrastructure code, many calls at once, one binary that you can build for any system. You build a binary; running it does not need Go. |

## Why not just `child_process`?

A process per call costs about 17.6 ms to start. A worker that is already running answers a small call in 0.07 ms (Python) or 0.03 ms (Rust and Go), and keeps your model in memory. Beyond speed you get what you would otherwise write yourself: a pool, a bounded queue, timeouts, cancellation, restart of workers that die, memory limits, streaming, binary transfer and the contracts that make a function an action. [Use cases](docs/use-cases.md) has the cases with their numbers, and [Where it does not fit](docs/use-cases.md#where-it-does-not-fit) says when not to use it.

## Install

TotalFusion is **not on npm yet**. From a clone of the repository:

```bash
npm install ../totalfusion
```

Once published it will be `npm install totalfusion`. It needs Node.js 20 or newer, and Python 3.9 or newer for the Python runtime. Rust and Go are needed only to build a worker in that language. **TotalFusion never installs, downloads or compiles anything for you.** → [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md)

## Examples

All of them run from a clone of the repository:

## Status

Version 0.1.0, not published. The whole test suite (more than 410 tests: Python, Rust, Go, WebAssembly and the components for Flow) **passes in GitHub Actions on Linux, macOS and Windows**, and it was run locally on macOS as well:

| | Where it has run |
|---|---|
| Linux | GitHub Actions on Ubuntu: Node.js 20, 22 and 24 with Python 3.9 to 3.14 |
| macOS | GitHub Actions (Node.js 24, Python 3.12) and locally on Apple silicon (Node.js 20, 22 and 24, Python 3.9 to 3.15) |
| Windows | GitHub Actions (Node.js 24, Python 3.12): the whole suite, including the binary pipes, the memory of a worker and the Rust, Go and WebAssembly workers |
| Rust | The stable toolchain of the runners, and 1.99 locally (the `totalfusion` crate and its worker) |
| Go | The stable toolchain of the runners on the three systems, and locally with Go 1.21 and 1.27 (the module with the race detector, and the 62 tests of its worker) |
| WebAssembly | GitHub Actions on the three systems (Node.js 20, 22 and 24 on Linux), and locally with Node.js 26: the 50 tests of the module, including a module that tries to get out |
| Flow | The test harness of Total.js on the three systems, and by hand in the designer of Flow 11.1 on macOS |
| Total.js | `total5` from npm (0.0.19) in GitHub Actions, and the development version 0.0.20-1 locally. **The MCP endpoint is not in 0.0.19**, so it is checked only against the development version, on macOS |

Python 3.15 and the combinations that are not in the matrix of [.github/workflows/test.yml](.github/workflows/test.yml) were run only locally.

Not verified: connecting a specific AI client to the MCP endpoint, and the components for Flow in the cloud service of Total.js.

<!-- AGENTS.md: AGENTS.md -->

# AGENTS.md

Guidance for AI coding agents. The first part is for an agent that **uses** TotalFusion in an application; the second is for one that **works on** this repository.

## Project

TotalFusion extends Total.js 5 with other runtimes: functions written in **Python, Rust, Go and WebAssembly** are called from Node.js as `async` functions, and become Total.js actions, API routes, MCP tools, Server-Sent Events and nodes of Flow. Each runtime is a pool of worker processes that Node.js supervises; a crash in a worker never takes the application down. The engine (`require('totalfusion')`) does not depend on Total.js; `fusion.register()`, `fusion.sse()` and `fusion.flow()` do.

Package name: `totalfusion` (version 0.1.0, not on npm yet)
Node.js: 20 or newer. No dependencies. Plain JavaScript, no TypeScript (Total.js does not support it: never add types or `.d.ts`).
License: MIT

## Using it

Install from a clone while it is not on npm: `npm install ../totalfusion`. The documentation is in `docs/` (start with `docs/getting-started.md`, the tutorials in `docs/tutorials/`, the options in `docs/reference.md`).

```js
const fusion = require('totalfusion');   // in a Total.js definition: REQUIRE('totalfusion')

fusion.configure({
	python: { path: './python', workers: 2 },        // a folder of .py files
	rust: { binary: './worker/target/release/worker' },
	go: { binary: './worker/worker' },
	wasm: { module: './module.wasm' }                // one module for each Fusion
});

await fusion.python('module.function', args);       // also fusion.rust(), fusion.go(), fusion.wasm()
for await (const chunk of fusion.python.stream('module.generator', args)) { }
```

- **Total.js:** `await fusion.register({ python: { path: PATH.root('python') }, watch: DEBUG })` turns every function that declares a contract into an action (`module/function`). Then `ROUTE('API /api/ +module_function --> module/function')`. Do not `require('totalfusion/total5')`: Total.js does not accept that form; everything is on the main package.
- **Contracts** are the schema syntax of Total.js: Python `@action(summary=..., input='*text:String', output=..., mcp=True)`; Rust `.summary().input().mcp(true)`; Go `.Summary().Input().MCP(true)`. A function without a contract is callable from JavaScript but is **not** an action. `*` means required.
- **Errors:** `ValueError` (Python), `Error::invalid` (Rust) and `Invalid` (Go) are mistakes of the caller: Total.js sends their message to the client. Every other failure answers "The action failed" and the detail goes to the log.
- **MCP:** only functions that say `mcp` become tools, and the endpoint (`$mcp : true` in `config`) has **no authentication** unless you add one. Never turn it on in an application that listens on a public address without authentication.
- **A worker's standard output carries the protocol.** In Python, Rust and Go the SDK redirects `print` and `fmt.Println` to the error output, but write to the error output on purpose.
- **WebAssembly** modules run in a sandbox (no files, no network, no environment) and are WASI reactors with a small ABI (`docs/webassembly.md`). A runtime has one module: use one `new Fusion({ wasm: ... })` for each module. The SDK is in Go (`app.Wasm()` in `init`, Go 1.24 or newer).
- **A route with a dot in a segment** (`/x/discount.apply/`) looks like a file to Total.js and gets an empty reply: split the function name across segments.
- **Nothing is downloaded, compiled or installed for you.** Workers are built by the user (`cargo build --release`, `go build`).
- **Check the setup first:** `npx totalfusion doctor --path ./python` (also `--runtime rust|go|wasm` with `--binary` or `--module`). For Python it reads the components without importing them; for Rust and Go it executes the worker with `--describe`, and for WebAssembly it runs the host to read the module contract. Use trusted native workers. It says what to fix; with `--json` it prints `{ ok, checks: [{ status, name, message, fix }] }` and the exit code is `0`, `1` (something to fix) or `2` (wrong usage). Run the command of `fix` instead of guessing.
- **Flow:** seven components (Python, Rust, Go, WebAssembly, Stream, Events, Stats) in `total5/flow/`, listed in `total5/flow/db.json`; see `docs/flow.md`.
- **More for models:** `llms.txt` (an index of the documentation), `llms-full.txt` (all of it in one file), `schemas/configure.schema.json` (the options of `fusion.configure()` and of a call) and `schemas/contract.schema.json` (a contract and what `--describe` prints). `docs/ai.md` explains them.

## Repository layout

Each area (`go/`, `rust/`, `python/`, `wasm/`, `total5/`, `tests/`) has its own `AGENTS.md` with the rules of that area: read it before you change files there.

- `index.js` is the `Fusion` class and the entry point. `lib/` is the engine: `pool.js` (workers, queue, timeouts, recycling, health check, retries), `protocol.js` (frames), `stream.js`, `watch.js`, `doctor.js`, `options.js`, `errors.js`.
- `python/`, `rust/`, `go/`, `wasm/` are the runtimes: each has an adapter (`index.js`) and its worker or SDK (`worker.py` and `sdk/`; the `totalfusion` crate in `rust/src`; the Go module in `go/*.go`; `wasm/host.js`).
- `total5/` is the Total.js integration: `index.js` (`register`, `sse`), `flow.js` and `flow/*.html` (the components of Flow).
- `bin/totalfusion.js` is the `doctor` command. `scripts/flow-db.js` builds `total5/flow/db.json`; `scripts/llms.js` builds `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`.
- For Codex: this file is the native entry point; no separate Codex instructions file is needed. Start the chat in the TotalFusion repository so instructions and repo-local skills are discovered. The four entries in `.agents/skills/` reuse the shared checklists in `.claude/skills/`; read their linked checklist when a workflow applies. See `docs/ai.md`.
- For agents: this file, `CLAUDE.md` and `GEMINI.md` (they import it), `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.claude/skills/` (four checklists: add a function, diagnose a worker, add a tutorial, verify a change) and `.claude/settings.json` (the commands that are safe to run without asking), `schemas/` and `llms.txt`.
- `tests/` has the tests and the workers they run (`tests/go`, `tests/rust`, `tests/wasm`, `tests/components`). `examples/` has the examples (`examples/README.md` lists them, and `tests/examples.test.js` runs them) and the applications of the tutorials (`examples/tutorials`). `docs/` is the documentation, and it is tested.
- `.github/workflows/test.yml` runs the suite on Linux (Node.js 20, 22, 24), macOS and Windows.

## Commands

```bash
npm test                                  # the whole suite (node --test)
npm run check                             # the fast checks: documentation, files for agents, package
npm run generate                          # llms.txt, llms-full.txt and total5/flow/db.json
node --test tests/go.test.js              # one file
npm run test:rust                         # cargo test of the crate
npm run test:go                           # go test of the module
node scripts/flow-db.js --write           # only the list of components of Flow
node scripts/llms.js --write              # only llms.txt and llms-full.txt
npx totalfusion doctor --path tests/components
npm pack --dry-run                        # what goes into the package
```

`npm test` needs Python 3.9 or newer. The tests of Rust run if `cargo` is found, the ones of Go if `go` is found (`GO=/path/to/go`), the ones of WebAssembly and the tutorial 2 if that Go is 1.24 or newer, and the ones of Total.js and Flow if Total.js 5 is found (`TOTAL5_PATH`, the `total5` package or a sibling `../framework5`). Without them those tests are skipped, not failed. See `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

## Conventions

- Plain JavaScript in the style of Total.js: tabs, `'use strict'`, no dependencies. Rust follows `rustfmt`, Go follows `gofmt`.
- The protocol is version 2 (`lib/protocol.js`): the Python worker, the Rust crate, the Go module and the host of WebAssembly all speak it. A change in one is a change in all.
- A change comes with tests, and a test must be able to fail: **break the code on purpose and see the test fail** before you trust it.
- The documentation is part of the product and is tested (`tests/docs.test.js`: links, anchors, titles, reachability). A new page goes in `docs/README.md` and in `PAGES` of `scripts/llms.js`; `tests/agents.test.js` fails if it is missing. Say what was measured and where, what was verified and what was not. Do not write numbers from memory: run it.
- A tutorial is a page in `docs/tutorials` and an application in `examples/tutorials` with the same name and a `verify.js`; `tests/tutorials.test.js` runs it. Write the outputs of the page from what the application printed.
- Every replacement that a script does must assert that its pattern matched: a silent no-op looks like success.

## Pitfalls

- **Windows:** an executable that is running cannot be replaced (the Rust and Go workers run from a copy: `shadowCopy`). In Go, never make a second `os.File` for a handle that another `os.File` owns: the finalizer of the first closes it at the first garbage collection (`go/stdout_windows.go`). Checkouts have CRLF line endings: split text with `/\r?\n/`.
- **Python:** run the tests with `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE` unset (`env -u PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE npm test`); the components are loaded from source, never from bytecode (`stale.test.js`).
- **Make failures loud.** A worker that exits silently hides its cause: print the reason to the error output and exit non-zero.
- **Processes:** a script that waits for workers or watchers needs its own keep-alive timer, because idle workers are `unref`'d. Tests that start an application must spawn it with an IPC channel (`stdio: [..., 'ipc']`), or Total.js starts its debug watcher and the process cannot be stopped cleanly.
- **Flow:** the icon font of Flow is not Tabler: use names from the icon list of Flow (public/icons-db.html in its repository) or nothing shows.
- **Do not commit** built workers or modules (`target/`, `plugins/*.wasm`, `__pycache__`, `*.js.map`), and leave no files in the temporary directory after the tests.

<!-- Using TotalFusion with AI assistants: docs/ai.md -->

# Using TotalFusion with AI assistants

Two things are in this page: how to give an assistant (or an agent) what it needs to **write code that uses TotalFusion**, and how your functions become **tools that an agent can call**. Every file mentioned here is kept true by a test of the project (`tests/agents.test.js`).

## What to give your assistant

| File | What it is | Give it when |
|---|---|---|
| [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) | Instructions: how to use TotalFusion in an application, how the repository is organised, the commands, and the pitfalls to avoid. It is also in the npm package, at `node_modules/totalfusion/AGENTS.md`. | The assistant works in your application or in this repository. |
| [llms.txt](../llms.txt) | An index of the documentation, in the format of [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org): one line and one link for each page. | The assistant can read links and you want it to choose what to read. |
| [llms-full.txt](../llms-full.txt) | All the documentation in one file. | The assistant cannot read links, or you want it to have everything at once. |
| [schemas/configure.schema.json](../schemas/configure.schema.json) | JSON Schema of `fusion.configure()` and of the options of a call. | To validate a configuration, or to let an editor complete it. |
| [schemas/contract.schema.json](../schemas/contract.schema.json) | JSON Schema of the contract of a function and of what a worker prints with `--describe`. | To write a worker in another language, or to check one. |

`llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt` are built from the pages of the repository (`node scripts/llms.js --write`), so they cannot be out of date: a test fails if they are.

If your assistant takes a block of instructions of your own, this is enough to start (it is the essence of `AGENTS.md`):

```
This project uses TotalFusion (https://github.com/totaljs-es/totalfusion) to call functions written in
Python, Rust, Go and WebAssembly from Total.js 5 and Node.js. Read node_modules/totalfusion/AGENTS.md first.
- A function that declares a contract (@action in Python, .summary().input() in Rust, .Summary().Input() in Go)
  becomes a Total.js action with fusion.register(); only functions that say mcp become tools for AI agents.
- The standard output of a worker carries the protocol: write to the error output.
- Check the setup with: npx totalfusion doctor --json
- A WebAssembly module runs in a sandbox (no files, no network, no environment); one module for each Fusion.
- The MCP endpoint has no authentication unless you add one: never expose it without.
```

## Your functions as tools for agents

A function with a contract and `mcp=True` (Python), `.mcp(true)` (Rust) or `.MCP(true)` (Go) is offered by the MCP endpoint of Total.js as a tool: its name, its description, the schema of its arguments and the schema of its result come **from the contract**, so you write them once. The [first tutorial](tutorials/01-python-action-and-mcp.md) does it from the start and shows the real answers of `tools/list` and `tools/call`.

Two things to decide before you do it for real: **which functions** the agent may call (an agent sees only what you say, so leave the rest without `mcp`), and **who may reach the endpoint** (it has no authentication unless you add one with `Total.mcp.auth`). See [Security](security.md).

## Let an agent check the environment

```bash
npx totalfusion doctor --json
```

It prints one JSON object, and the exit code says the result: `0` when everything is in order, `1` when something has to be fixed, `2` for a wrong usage.

```json
{
  "runtime": "python",
  "ok": false,
  "checks": [
    { "status": "error", "name": "Libraries", "message": "numpy used by stats needs to be installed", "fix": "/project/.venv/bin/python -m pip install numpy" }
  ],
  "text": "TotalFusion doctor: python ..."
}
```

Each check has a `status` (`ok`, `warn` or `error`), a `name`, a `message` and, when there is something to do, the exact command in `fix`. An agent can run the command of `fix` instead of guessing. For Python, the doctor reads components without importing them. For Rust and Go it executes the worker with `--describe`; for WebAssembly the host reads the module contract inside its sandbox. A native worker still has the permissions of its user during discovery: use a trusted binary. See [Development and diagnosis](development.md).

## For agents that work on the repository

The repository has the files that the common agents look for. They all lead to the same instructions, so there is only one text to keep true:

- `AGENTS.md`: the instructions. Each area of the repository (`go`, `rust`, `python`, `wasm`, `total5`, `tests`) has its own, with a `CLAUDE.md` that imports it, because Claude Code loads the `CLAUDE.md` of a folder when it works there.
- Codex reads `AGENTS.md` directly. Its four repo-local skill entry points are in `.agents/skills/`, and each links to the corresponding checklist in `.claude/skills/`. The checklist stays in one place.
- `CLAUDE.md` and `GEMINI.md`: they import `AGENTS.md`.
- `.github/copilot-instructions.md`: a short version for GitHub Copilot, with the rules that matter most.
- `.claude/skills/`: four skills for Claude Code (add a function to an application, diagnose a worker that fails, add a tutorial, verify a change). Each one is a checklist with the real commands.
- `.claude/settings.json`: the commands that are safe to run without asking (the tests, `npm run check`, read-only git).

## Codex

Start a Codex chat with this repository as the workspace. Codex reads the root `AGENTS.md` and instructions along the path to its working directory. When working in another area, read that area's `AGENTS.md` before editing it. If your chat started in another project, explicitly read this repository's instructions; mentioning its path does not change the chat's workspace.

The skills in `.agents/skills/` expose the same four workflows as Claude Code: add a function, diagnose a worker, add a tutorial and verify a change. Codex can select one when its description matches the task; you can also ask for it explicitly, for example `$totalfusion-diagnose-worker`. Each entry links to the maintained checklist, so updates to it apply to both agents.

The shared `.claude/settings.json` configures Claude Code. Codex uses the permissions of its own environment; these repository instructions do not grant filesystem access, network access or command approval. No Codex configuration change is required to read the instructions and skills.

For applications that install TotalFusion as a dependency, ask Codex to read `node_modules/totalfusion/AGENTS.md`; dependency instructions are not automatically loaded as application instructions. The repo-local skills are for a checkout of TotalFusion and are not shipped in its npm package.

See the official OpenAI documentation on [AGENTS.md](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/agents-md) and [skills](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills) for discovery and invocation.

## What is verified

`tests/agents.test.js` checks that the paths and the commands that `AGENTS.md` and the skills mention exist, that `llms.txt` lists every page and that its links lead to files that exist, that `llms-full.txt` is what the pages say, that the schemas have the same options as the code, and that the files for each agent lead to `AGENTS.md`. It also checks that every Codex skill has the same discovery metadata as its shared checklist and that its link resolves to that checklist. What is **not** verified is how a given assistant uses these files: that depends on the assistant.

---

<!-- Getting started: docs/getting-started.md -->

# Getting started

## 1. Install

TotalFusion is **not on npm yet**. From a clone of the repository, install it by its path:

```bash
npm install ../totalfusion          # or "totalfusion": "file:../totalfusion" in your package.json
```

Once it is published it will be `npm install totalfusion`. You need Node.js 20 or newer, and Python 3.9 or newer for the Python runtime. Rust and Go are needed only to **build** a worker in that language, never to run one.

## 2. Your first function, in any Node.js program

```python
# python/hello.py
def greet(data):
    return {'message': 'Hello ' + data['name']}
```

```js
// app.js
const fusion = require('totalfusion');

fusion.configure({ python: { path: './python' } });

fusion.python('hello.greet', { name: 'world' }).then(result => {
    console.log(result);            // { message: 'Hello world' }
    return fusion.shutdown();
});
```

A pool of Python processes starts on the first call and stays alive. [examples/basic.js](../examples/basic.js) is a version of this that you can run.

## 3. In a Total.js 5 application

Declare what the function takes and returns, and it becomes an **action** of Total.js:

```python
# python/hello.py
from totalfusion import action

@action(summary='Greets someone', input='*name:String', output='message:String')
def greet(data):
    return {'message': 'Hello ' + data['name']}
```

```js
// definitions/fusion.js
const fusion = REQUIRE('totalfusion');

exports.install = function() {
    fusion.register({ python: { path: PATH.root('python') }, watch: DEBUG });
    ROUTE('API  /api/  +hello_greet  -->  hello/greet');
};
```

Now `ACTION('hello/greet', { name: 'x' })` and `POST /api/` work, Total.js rejects an input without `name` before Python runs, and with `watch: DEBUG` the next request uses your edits. The whole application is in [examples/totaljs-app](../examples/totaljs-app). More in [Total.js 5](total5.md).

## 4. Rust

If a function is heavy on the CPU, write it in Rust, build a binary and call it the same way:

```js
fusion.configure({ rust: { binary: './worker/target/release/worker' } });
await fusion.rust('collatz.longest', { limit: 3000000 });
```

See [Rust](rust.md) and [examples/rust.js](../examples/rust.js).

## 5. Go

If a function is network or infrastructure code, or you want one binary that you can build for any system, write it in Go and call it the same way:

```js
fusion.configure({ go: { binary: './worker/worker' } });
await fusion.go('net.check', { host: 'example.com' });
```

See [Go](go.md) and [examples/go.js](../examples/go.js).

## 6. Check your setup

```bash
npx totalfusion doctor --path ./python
```

It tells you which libraries are missing and the exact command to install them in the right Python. Nothing is imported, run or installed. See [Development and diagnosis](development.md).

## Where to go next

| If you want to... | Read |
|---|---|
| use machine learning or any Python library | [Python](python.md) |
| run heavy work without blocking Node.js | [Rust](rust.md) or [Go](go.md) |
| expose functions as actions, API routes, MCP tools | [Total.js 5](total5.md) |
| send images, audio or arrays | [Binary data](binary-data.md) |
| show a model's output as it is produced | [Streaming](streaming.md) |
| call many slow things at the same time | [Working with the workers](workers.md#several-calls-at-the-same-time) |
| see ideas with real numbers | [Use cases](use-cases.md) |
| know what a setting does | [Reference](reference.md) |

---

<!-- Use cases: docs/use-cases.md -->

# Use cases

Each case says **what was run** and what was measured, so you can tell a result from an idea. All the numbers come from one machine (8 cores, macOS, Node.js 24), and they show orders of magnitude, not guarantees.

## Machine-learning inference behind an API

**Goal:** a model that lives in Python, served as an action of Total.js.

**How:** load the model in `@startup`, declare the contract, `preload` it, and `warmup` at boot.

```python
@startup
def load():
    global pipe
    pipe = pipeline('sentiment-analysis', model=MODEL)

@action(summary='Detects the sentiment of a text', input='*text:String', output='label:String\nscore:Number', mcp=True)
def analyze(data):
    return pipe(data['text'])[0]
```

**Run and measured:** DistilBERT with PyTorch ([examples/components/sentiment.py](../examples/components/sentiment.py)). A call takes about 5 to 7 ms once the worker is warm; the first request after `warmup` through the MCP endpoint took about 22 ms; each worker uses 1.35 GB, so start with one or two. A scikit-learn forest ([classifier.py](../examples/components/classifier.py)) answered in 7 ms. See [Models and memory](python.md#models-and-memory).

## Let AI agents call your functions

**Goal:** an agent can use a function of yours as a tool, with the arguments checked.

**How:** add `mcp=True` (`.mcp(true)` in Rust, `.MCP(true)` in Go) to the contract and enable the MCP endpoint of Total.js. The tool and its schema come from the contract.

**Run:** the endpoint was called with `tools/list` and `tools/call`: only the functions that say `mcp` are listed, the schema has the `input`, `query` and `params` sections, an invalid argument is rejected by Total.js, and a function that does not say `mcp` answers "Unknown tool". Remember that the endpoint has no authentication unless you add it: see [Security](security.md).

## Show a model's output as it is produced

**Goal:** the user sees the text of a language model while it is generated, and the model stops if they leave.

**How:** a Python generator (`yield` per token) and `fusion.sse($, stream)` in a route.

```python
def generate(data):
    for token in model.generate(data['prompt']):
        yield token
```

```js
ROUTE('GET /generate/', $ => fusion.sse($, fusion.python.stream('llm.generate', { prompt: $.query.prompt })));
```

**Run and measured:** a real model (DistilGPT2, CPU, [generate.py](../examples/components/generate.py)) gave the first token after 61 ms and a new one every 7 ms, and cutting the stream after 5 tokens of a 500-token request stopped the generation in 43 ms. The Server-Sent Events route was run in a Total.js application with a Python generator (one event every 0.4 s, the generator is cancelled when the browser leaves). The two pieces were not chained in one test with the language model. See [Streaming](streaming.md).

## Heavy CPU work without blocking Node.js

**Goal:** a calculation that takes seconds must not freeze the application.

**How:** write it in Rust or Go and call it with `fusion.rust(...)` or `fusion.go(...)`; let one process use all the cores with `concurrency`.

**Measured:** the longest Collatz chain below 3 million, the same algorithm in each language. Optimized JavaScript takes 1.2 s and Rust 0.33 s (3.6 times faster; the naive JavaScript is 14 times slower than Rust), and pure Python is 48 times slower than Rust. Eight of those jobs take 9.1 s in JavaScript **blocking the event loop the whole time**, against 0.7 s on four Rust workers with 1 ms of delay in the event loop. The same test run again with a Go worker next to the Rust one, on the same day and machine (three alternating runs, and another implementation of the optimized JavaScript, 0.95 s): Go took 0.48 to 0.50 s and Rust 0.36 s, and eight jobs took 7.5 s in JavaScript against 1.0 to 1.1 s on four Go workers and 0.75 to 0.84 s on four Rust workers. See [Rust](rust.md), [Go](go.md) and the examples in [examples/rust](../examples/rust) and [examples/go](../examples/go).

## Vector search and numerical work with NumPy

**Goal:** use NumPy (or any numerical library) from Node.js without paying a process start per call.

**Measured:** nearest neighbours over 50,000 vectors of 128 dimensions ([vectors.py](../examples/components/vectors.py)): the worker builds the index once (about 145 ms), then every call takes about 3 ms, against about 98 ms when a process is started per call. An array of 10 million `float32` (40 MB) makes the round trip in 18 ms as a `Float32Array`, with no base64 and no JSON. See [Binary data](binary-data.md).

## Call slow things at the same time

**Goal:** many calls that spend their time waiting (an API, a database) should not each need a process.

**How:** `async def` functions in Python and `concurrency: N`.

**Measured:** 64 calls that wait 0.2 s each take 3.23 s on 4 workers with one call at a time, and 0.21 s with `concurrency: 64` on a single worker that uses 24 MB instead of 94 MB. See [Several calls at the same time](workers.md#several-calls-at-the-same-time).

## Send big files and arrays without base64

**Goal:** images, audio or arrays go to a worker and come back, and the transfer does not dominate.

**Measured:** a 1 MB buffer makes the round trip in 0.5 ms, 32 MB in 14 ms and 100 MB in 43 ms; as base64 inside JSON the same bytes take 4.4 ms and 145 ms for 1 MB and 32 MB, and 100 MB does not fit (it exceeds the JSON limit). A sketch of an image function (`Image.open(io.BytesIO(data['image']))` and back) is in [Binary data](binary-data.md); that sketch was not run, the transfer was.

## Edit the code while the application runs

**Goal:** see the effect of a change in the next call, with no restart.

**Run:** in [examples/totaljs-app](../examples/totaljs-app), editing `python/words.py` while the application ran changed the answer of the next request (a count of 3 became 300), and no call was lost. In the tests, calls made while the workers were being replaced all succeeded. See [Development](development.md).

## Several runtimes in the same application

**Run:** both runtimes can be configured in the same `fusion` and called side by side, each with its own pool (`fusion.python(...)`, `fusion.rust(...)` and `fusion.go(...)`). A pipeline that chains them (for example a model in Python and a post-processing step in Rust) was **not** built as an example.

## Where it does not fit

- **Light work on small data.** JavaScript in the same process pays no transfer: it wins. A call to a worker costs 0.03 ms (Rust and Go) to 0.07 ms (Python) of overhead, which is nothing for real work and everything for adding two numbers.
- **Code you do not trust.** A worker is not a sandbox: see [Security](security.md).
- **Very many Node.js processes.** Every process has its own pool of workers, so with the cluster mode of Total.js the workers (and their models) multiply by the number of processes.

---

<!-- Python: docs/python.md -->

# Python

Write functions in Python and call them from Node.js and Total.js as `async` functions. Python is the right choice when you need its ecosystem: machine learning, scientific computing, data processing, any library that only exists for Python.

## Quick start

```python
# python/analyzer.py
from totalfusion import action

@action(summary='Counts the words of a text', input='*text:String', output='words:Number', mcp=True)
def analyze(data):
    return {'words': len(data['text'].split())}
```

```js
// any Node.js program
const fusion = require('totalfusion');
const result = await fusion.python('analyzer.analyze', { text: 'Hello world' });   // { words: 2 }
```

```js
// a Total.js application: the function becomes the action 'analyzer/analyze'
await REQUIRE('totalfusion').register({ python: { path: PATH.root('python') } });
```

## Requirements and the environment

- **Python 3.9 or newer.** The test suite has been run on 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14 and 3.15. The worker uses only the standard library.
- **TotalFusion never installs anything.** You create the environment and install the libraries your components need.
- **The interpreter** is chosen in this order: the `python` option, the `venv` option, the `TOTALFUSION_PYTHON` variable, then `python3` (`python` on Windows).
- **Use a virtual environment.** The libraries you install are then yours alone:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install numpy scikit-learn
```

```js
fusion.configure({ python: { path: './python', venv: './.venv' } });
```

- **Check it** before running anything with `npx totalfusion doctor --path ./python --venv ./.venv`: it tells you which libraries are missing and the exact command to install them in the right Python. See [Development and diagnosis](development.md#checking-your-setup).

## Writing components

A component is a Python module inside `path`. Every public function defined in it can be called from Node.js with one argument (any JSON value) and returns any JSON value. Functions can be `def` or `async def`.

- Use `__all__` to expose an explicit list instead.
- Names starting with `_` and names imported from other modules are not callable.
- Modules outside `path` (standard library, site-packages) cannot be called. Import them from your own component instead.
- `print()` and anything written to stdout goes to stderr, so it never breaks the protocol.
- **Components are always loaded from their source.** Python trusts a `.pyc` when the modification time of the source (in whole seconds) and its size have not changed, so a file saved twice within a second without changing its size would keep running the old code, even in a new worker. TotalFusion never reads or writes bytecode for your components, which also means it never leaves a `__pycache__` next to your files. The libraries you import (NumPy, PyTorch, the standard library) keep their own bytecode.

## Contracts and hooks

```python
from totalfusion import action, startup, shutdown

model = None

@startup
def load():                       # once per worker, right after the module is imported
    global model
    model = load_my_model()

@shutdown
def unload():                     # when the worker stops gracefully (1.5 s at most)
    model.close()

@action(summary='Classifies a text', input='*text:String // Text to classify', output='label:String', mcp=True)
def classify(data):
    return { 'label': model.predict(data['text']) }
```

`@action` declares the contract: `summary`, `input`, `output`, `query`, `params` (Total.js schema syntax), `mcp`, `permissions`, `user`, `sa`, `su`, `idempotent`, `timeout` and `name`/`id`. Its arguments are read **statically** (they must be literals), so `fusion.describe('python')` lists every contract without importing your code and without loading any model.

`@startup` and `@shutdown` can be `def` or `async def`. To load a model **before** the worker reports ready (so the first call is not slow), name the module in `preload`: `fusion.configure({ python: { preload: ['classifier'] } })`. A module that cannot be preloaded fails the start with the real traceback in `err.stderr`.

## Models and memory

Every worker is a separate process with **its own copy of the model**, so memory grows with `workers`. Measured on a MacBook (8 cores, Python 3.12, physical footprint from `footprint`, not `ps`, which under-reports compressed memory on macOS):

| Model | Per worker | 1 worker | 2 workers | 4 workers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| scikit-learn random forest ([classifier.py](../examples/components/classifier.py)) | 129 MB | 150 calls/s | - | 554 calls/s (516 MB) |
| DistilBERT sentiment with PyTorch ([sentiment.py](../examples/components/sentiment.py)) | 1.35 GB | 186 calls/s | 274-309 calls/s (2.7 GB) | 334-366 calls/s (5.4 GB) |

The DistilBERT call takes about 5-7 ms for a sentence and 25 ms for 1,900 characters. A worker is ready in about 2.5 s (PyTorch import plus the model, from a warm disk cache), against 2.7-3.3 s **per call** when a process is spawned each time.

What to do with it:

- **Small models:** one worker per core you want to use scales almost linearly.
- **Large models:** start with `workers: 1` or `2`. PyTorch already uses several threads inside one process, so four workers gave +20% throughput over two for twice the memory. Setting `OMP_NUM_THREADS` through the `env` option did not change that noticeably.
- **Use `preload`.** The `timeout` of a call starts when it is sent to a worker, so a model loaded lazily on the first call would count its loading time against that call. With `preload` the worker reports ready only after loading, and the load has its own limit (`startTimeout`, 30 s by default, raise it for big models).
- **Use `warmup`.** Workers start with the first call. `await fusion.warmup('python')` (or `fusion.register({ warmup: true })`) starts them all at boot, so the first request does not wait for the model: the first request through MCP went from 2.4 s to about 22 ms (later ones take 9-12 ms), with the boot taking the 2.6 s instead.
- **Keep input shapes fixed.** PyTorch on CPU prepares its kernels per tensor shape, and the first call with each new sequence length took 130-250 ms. Padding to a fixed length in `@startup` and in the function removed every slow call (40 different sentences, all between 7 and 9 ms). See [sentiment.py](../examples/components/sentiment.py).

## How a call runs

- A function receives **one argument**, any JSON value (usually a dict), and returns any JSON value. `def` and `async def` are both fine, and a function that yields is a [stream](streaming.md).
- `async def` functions run in the event loop of the worker and overlap. `def` functions run in a pool of threads, as many as `concurrency` allows (at least 8).
- With `concurrency: 1`, the default, a worker runs one call at a time and the work is spread over the processes. See [Several calls at the same time](workers.md#several-calls-at-the-same-time) for what changes when you raise it: calls that overlap in a worker **share the state of its modules**, and because of the GIL, computation in pure Python does not speed up with threads (use more workers for it).
- A `def` function cannot be interrupted. After a timeout the caller is rejected at once, and if the function does not return within `cancelGrace` the worker is killed and replaced. An `async def` function is cancelled for real. See [Errors and cancellation](errors.md#cancellation).
- **Components are loaded from their source every time.** Edit a file and the next worker runs the new code, even if you saved twice within a second.

## What crosses the boundary

| JavaScript | Python |
|---|---|
| object, array, string, number, boolean, `null` | `dict`, `list`, `str`, `int` or `float`, `bool`, `None` |
| `Buffer`, `Uint8Array`, `ArrayBuffer` | `bytes` |
| `Float32Array`, `Float64Array`, `Int32Array`... | `memoryview` of the matching type, without copying |

From Python, `bytes`, `bytearray`, `memoryview`, `array.array` and anything with the buffer protocol (NumPy arrays included) go back as a `Buffer` or the matching typed array. Tuples go back as arrays. A value that is not JSON (a `set`, an object of your own) fails with `NOT_SERIALIZABLE`, and so do `NaN` and infinity. See [Binary data](binary-data.md) for the details and the numbers.

## Options of the Python runtime

`path`, `venv`, `python`, `preload` and `requirements` are specific to Python. `workers`, `concurrency`, `timeout`, `maxQueue`, `startTimeout`, `cancelGrace`, `maxCalls`, `maxMemory`, `healthInterval`, `healthTimeout`, `forwardStderr` and `env` are shared. All of them are in the [reference](reference.md#options).

## When something goes wrong

| What you see | Why, and what to do |
|---|---|
| `ModuleNotFoundError` | A library is not installed **in the Python that runs the workers**. `err.hint` has the command to install it there. |
| `NOT_FOUND` for a function that exists | Only public functions defined in modules inside `path` can be called: names that start with `_`, names imported from other modules and modules outside `path` are not exposed. |
| The first call is slow | The model loads when the worker starts. Use `preload` and `fusion.warmup('python')` so it loads at boot. |
| `print()` shows up in the terminal of the application | What a worker writes to its standard output goes to the error output, so it never breaks the protocol. `forwardStderr: false` hides it. |
| Memory grows over the days | Libraries for machine learning tend to leak: use `maxCalls` or `maxMemory` and the worker is replaced without losing a call. See [Keeping workers healthy](workers.md#keeping-workers-healthy). |
| A call never returns | Set a `timeout`. A `def` function that cannot be cancelled costs its worker. |

---

<!-- Rust: docs/rust.md -->

# Rust

Write the functions in Rust, build a binary, and call it like the Python ones. A Rust worker is an **isolated process** that speaks the same protocol, so everything in this documentation applies to it as well: the pool, timeouts, cancellation, [binary data](binary-data.md), [streaming](streaming.md), [recycling and health checks](workers.md#keeping-workers-healthy), Total.js actions, MCP tools and the `doctor`.

## Write a worker

```rust
// rust/src/main.rs
use totalfusion::{object, App, Call, Error};

fn main() {
    App::new()
        .function("collatz.longest", |call: &Call| {
            let limit = call.args["limit"].as_i64().ok_or_else(|| Error::invalid("limit must be a number"))?;
            Ok(object! { "number" => limit })   // the real work goes here
        })
        .summary("Finds the number with the longest Collatz chain")
        .input("*limit:Number")
        .mcp(true)
        .run();
}
```

## Build it and call it

The crate is not on crates.io: the npm package ships its sources, so the `Cargo.toml` of your worker points to them:

```toml
[dependencies]
totalfusion = { path = "../node_modules/totalfusion/rust" }
```

```bash
cargo build --release
```

```js
fusion.configure({ rust: { binary: './rust/target/release/worker', workers: 4 } });

const result = await fusion.rust('collatz.longest', { limit: 3000000 });

for await (const chunk of fusion.rust.stream('count.up', { n: 10 })) { /* a function registered with .stream() */ }

// Total.js: the functions that declare their contract become actions
await fusion.register({ runtime: 'rust', rust: { binary: './rust/target/release/worker' } });
```

The guide of the crate, with the whole API, is in [rust/README.md](../rust/README.md). A complete example is in [examples/rust](../examples/rust).

## Good to know

- **Nothing is compiled for you.** `binary` is the path of a worker you built (or got precompiled), so the people who only run the application do not need Rust. `fusion.doctor('rust')` and `npx totalfusion doctor --binary ./worker` check that the file exists, can be executed, answers, speaks the same protocol version and is not a debug build.
- **A panic fails one call, not the worker.** A crash of the process is a `WORKER_CRASHED` error and the worker is replaced; Node.js never goes down.
- **Same options as Python:** `workers`, `concurrency`, `timeout`, `maxQueue`, `maxCalls`, `maxMemory`, `healthInterval`, `cancelGrace`... plus `args`, `env` and `cwd` for the process. Every call of a worker runs in its own thread, so `concurrency` makes one process use all the cores (see [Several calls at the same time](workers.md#several-calls-at-the-same-time)).
- **Contracts are declared in code**, with the same names as `@action` in Python (`summary`, `input`, `output`, `query`, `params`, `permissions`, `mcp`...). The binary prints them with `--describe`.
- **Where Rust pays off.** Heavy CPU work that should not block Node.js and that can use several cores. For the longest Collatz chain below 3 million (the same algorithm in each language, eight cores): optimized JavaScript takes 1.2 s and Rust 0.33 s (3.6x; the naive JavaScript most people write is 14x slower than Rust), and pure Python is 48x slower than Rust. Eight of those jobs take 9.1 s in JavaScript, **blocking the event loop the whole time**, and 0.7 s on four Rust workers, which leave the event loop free (1 ms of delay). A call that does nothing costs 0.03 ms. For light work on small data, JavaScript in the same process wins: it pays no transfer.
- **Windows:** the SDK points the standard output of the process to the error output, as it does on Unix, so `println!` is harmless. Windows does not let anything overwrite an executable that is running, so on Windows the worker runs from a **copy** (in the temporary folder, named after the time and size of your build) and the file you build stays free: `cargo build` can replace it while the workers are running, and `fusion.watch('rust')` picks the new build up. The copies of old builds are removed. `shadowCopy: true` does the same on any system, `shadowCopy: false` turns it off. The tests of the project run this on Windows.

## Rust or Python

| | Python | Rust |
|---|---|---|
| What it is for | The ecosystem: machine learning, scientific computing, any Python library | Speed, many threads, a small footprint |
| Work per call | Calls overlap in the event loop or in threads, and the GIL limits pure-Python computation | Every call runs in its own thread: one process can use all the cores |
| Memory of a minimal worker | 24 MB (measured with the components of the tests) | 1 MB (measured with the example worker) |
| What you ship | Your `.py` files, and Python with its libraries on the machine | One binary. The machine does not need Rust |
| Change it while the app runs | Save the file | Build again (`cargo build --release`): `fusion.watch('rust')` replaces the workers |
| Contracts | `@action(...)` | `.summary().input().output()...` in code |

They can be used in the same application: each runtime has its own pool, and `fusion.python(...)` and `fusion.rust(...)` are independent.

## The API of the crate

The whole API, with every method, is in [rust/README.md](../rust/README.md). In short:

- `App::new().function(name, |call| ...)` registers a function that answers once, and `.stream(name, |call| ...)` one that sends chunks with `call.emit(value)?`.
- `call.args` is the argument as a `Value`; `call.args["key"]` never panics. `call.is_cancelled()` tells a long function that Node.js gave up.
- `Error::invalid("...")` is a mistake of the caller (Total.js sends its message to the client); `Error::new("...")` is a failure that stays in the log. A panic fails one call, never the worker.
- `.on_shutdown(|| ...)` runs when the worker is asked to stop. What you do in `main` before `run()` happens before the worker says it is ready.
- The metadata methods apply to the function registered just before them: `summary`, `input`, `output`, `query`, `params`, `permissions`, `user`, `sa`, `su`, `idempotent`, `timeout`, `id`, `mcp` and `action`.

---

<!-- The Rust crate: rust/README.md -->

# totalfusion (Rust)

Write functions in Rust and call them from Node.js and Total.js as `async` functions. This crate is the Rust side of [TotalFusion](../README.md): your program registers its functions and TotalFusion starts it, keeps a pool of workers, and talks to it through the standard input and output.

A worker is a normal binary and an **isolated process**: a panic fails only the call that caused it, and even a crash of the whole process never takes Node.js down. Nothing is compiled by TotalFusion: you build the worker (`cargo build --release`) or you get it precompiled.

```rust
use totalfusion::{object, App, Call, Error};

fn main() {
    App::new()
        .function("text.length", |call: &Call| {
            let text = call.args["text"].as_str().ok_or_else(|| Error::invalid("text must be a string"))?;
            Ok(object! { "length" => text.chars().count() })
        })
        .summary("Counts the characters of a text")
        .input("*text:String")
        .output("length:Number")
        .mcp(true)
        .run();
}
```

```js
fusion.configure({ rust: { binary: './rust/target/release/worker', workers: 4 } });

await fusion.rust('text.length', { text: 'Hello' });   // { length: 5 }
```

## Functions

- `.function(name, |call| -> Result<Value, Error>)` answers once.
- `.stream(name, |call| -> Result<(), Error>)` sends many chunks with `call.emit(value)?`. In JavaScript: `for await (const chunk of fusion.rust.stream(name, args))`. `emit` waits when the consumer is slow (backpressure) and fails when it stops reading, so `?` ends the stream.
- `call.args` is a `Value`. `call.args["key"]` never panics: a missing member is `Null`.
- `call.is_cancelled()` is true when Node.js gave up (timeout, abort). A long function should look at it from time to time. A function that never looks is killed after `cancelGrace` and the worker is replaced.
- `.on_shutdown(|| ...)` runs when the worker is asked to stop. What you do in `main` before `run()` (load a model, open a connection) happens before the worker says it is ready.

## Values

`Value` holds everything JSON can, plus binary data that never goes through JSON. `Vec<u8>` is a `Buffer` in JavaScript, `Vec<f32>` is a `Float32Array`, and so on for `i8`, `i16`, `u16`, `i32`, `u32`, `i64` (`BigInt64Array`), `u64` and `f64`. Build objects with `object! { "key" => value }` and arrays with `Value::array([1, 2, 3])`; read them with `as_str()`, `as_f64()`, `as_i64()`, `as_bool()`, `as_bytes()`, `as_f32s()`, `as_f64s()`, `as_i32s()`, `as_array()` and `as_object()`.

NaN and infinity cannot be sent (JSON has no such numbers): the call fails with `NOT_SERIALIZABLE`.

## Errors

`Error::new("...")` is a failure of the function. `Error::invalid("...")` is a mistake of the caller (bad input): in Total.js its message is sent to the client, and the message of any other error stays in the log. `Error::named("DatabaseError", "...").with_code("E_DB")` gives the error a name and a code of its own. A panic becomes an error named `Panic`.

## Total.js

The methods that describe a function apply to the function registered just before them: `summary`, `input`, `output`, `query`, `params` (the schema syntax of Total.js, `*` means required), `permissions`, `user`, `sa`, `su`, `timeout`, `idempotent` (the call may be repeated on another worker if this one dies), `id` and `mcp`. A function that declares any of them, or calls `.action()`, becomes an action of Total.js with `fusion.register({ runtime: 'rust', rust: { binary } })`; the others stay callable from JavaScript but private. `mcp(true)` also exposes it to AI agents.

`./worker --describe` prints the contracts as JSON. This is what `register()` and `fusion.doctor('rust')` read: no function is called to learn them, but the program starts, so what your `main` does before `run()` (loading a model, opening a connection) runs too.

## Do not print to the standard output

It carries the protocol. On Unix and on Windows the crate redirects it to the error output for you, so `println!` is harmless, but use `eprintln!` to be safe everywhere. (This is tested on Windows in the continuous integration of the project.)

## Rebuilding while the application runs

Windows does not let anything overwrite an executable that is running, so on Windows TotalFusion runs your worker from a copy and the file `cargo build` writes stays free (`shadowCopy`, on by default there). With `fusion.watch('rust')` the workers are replaced by the new build.

## Requirements

Rust 2021 edition. The only dependency is `serde_json`. Tested with Rust 1.99 on macOS (Apple silicon), and in the continuous integration on Linux, macOS and Windows.

---

<!-- Go: docs/go.md -->

# Go

Write the functions in Go, build a binary, and call it like the Python and the Rust ones. A Go worker is an **isolated process** that speaks the same protocol, so everything in this documentation applies to it as well: the pool, timeouts, cancellation, [binary data](binary-data.md), [streaming](streaming.md), [recycling and health checks](workers.md#keeping-workers-healthy), Total.js actions, MCP tools and the `doctor`.

## Write a worker

```go
// worker/main.go
package main

import (
	totalfusion "github.com/totaljs-es/totalfusion/go"
)

func main() {
	app := totalfusion.New()

	app.Function("net.check", func(call *totalfusion.Call) (any, error) {
		host, ok := call.Args.Get("host").AsString()
		if !ok {
			return nil, totalfusion.Invalid("host must be a string")
		}
		return map[string]any{"host": host, "up": true}, nil // the real work goes here
	}).Summary("Checks if a host answers").Input("*host:String").MCP(true)

	app.Run()
}
```

## Build it and call it

The module is not on a registry: the npm package ships its sources, so the `go.mod` of your worker points to them:

```
module worker

go 1.21

require github.com/totaljs-es/totalfusion/go v0.0.0

replace github.com/totaljs-es/totalfusion/go => ../node_modules/totalfusion/go
```

```bash
cd worker && go build -o worker
```

```js
fusion.configure({ go: { binary: './worker/worker', workers: 4 } });

const result = await fusion.go('net.check', { host: 'example.com' });

for await (const chunk of fusion.go.stream('count.up', { n: 10 })) { /* a function registered with app.Stream() */ }

// Total.js: the functions that declare their contract become actions
await fusion.register({ runtime: 'go', go: { binary: './worker/worker' } });
```

The guide of the module, with the whole API, is in [go/README.md](../go/README.md). A complete example is in [examples/go](../examples/go).

## Good to know

- **Nothing is compiled for you.** `binary` is the path of a worker you built (or got precompiled), so the people who only run the application do not need Go. `fusion.doctor('go')` and `npx totalfusion doctor --runtime go --binary ./worker` check that the file exists, can be executed, answers and speaks the same protocol version.
- **It compiles for any system from any system.** The module is pure Go (no `cgo`), so `GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build` produces a Linux worker on your Mac, with no extra toolchain. The module is compiled and tested on Linux, macOS and Windows in the continuous integration, and it was checked with `go vet` for FreeBSD from macOS. A binary built for another system is the most common mistake, so the `doctor` reads the header of the worker, says for which system it was built (Linux, macOS or Windows, and the architecture) and gives the `GOOS` and `GOARCH` that build it for this one, without running it. An x64 worker on a Mac with Apple silicon or on Windows on ARM is only a warning: it runs emulated.
- **A panic fails one call, not the worker.** The stack goes to the error output (which Node.js shows) and the call fails with an error named `Panic`. A crash of the process is a `WORKER_CRASHED` error and the worker is replaced; Node.js never goes down.
- **Same options as the other runtimes:** `workers`, `concurrency`, `timeout`, `maxQueue`, `maxCalls`, `maxMemory`, `healthInterval`, `cancelGrace`... plus `args`, `env` and `cwd` for the process. Every call of a worker runs in its own goroutine, so `concurrency` makes one process use all the cores (see [Several calls at the same time](workers.md#several-calls-at-the-same-time)).
- **Cancellation is a `context.Context`.** `call.Context()` is cancelled when Node.js gives up on the call (a timeout, an `AbortSignal`, a consumer that leaves a stream), so you can pass it to a database or an HTTP request and the work stops. `call.Cancelled()` is the same as a boolean.
- **Contracts are declared in code**, with the same names as `@action` in Python (`Summary`, `Input`, `Output`, `Query`, `Params`, `Permissions`, `MCP`...). The binary prints them with `--describe`.
- **Where Go pays off.** Heavy CPU work that should not block Node.js and that can use several cores, and the code that Go is good at: network tools, scanners, pipelines, anything with a Go library. For the longest Collatz chain below 3 million (the same algorithm in each language, eight cores, macOS, three alternating runs on the same day): optimized JavaScript takes 0.95 s, Go 0.48 to 0.50 s (1.9x faster than JavaScript) and [Rust](rust.md) 0.36 s, so for this loop Rust is about 1.35 times faster than Go. Eight of those jobs take 7.5 s in JavaScript, **blocking the event loop the whole time**, and 1.0 to 1.1 s on four Go workers (0.75 to 0.84 s on four Rust workers), which leave the event loop free (0.4 to 4.9 ms of delay in the three Go runs). A call that does nothing costs 0.03 ms. For light work on small data, JavaScript in the same process wins: it pays no transfer.
- **The memory of a worker.** A minimal Go worker uses about 11 MB (the worker of the tests, measured with `ps`), because the Go runtime brings its own. `Memory()` reports the resident memory on Linux and the private bytes on Windows. On macOS, where asking the system for the footprint needs `cgo`, it reports the memory that the Go runtime holds, which is what a worker written in Go uses and agrees with `ps` within a megabyte in the measurement; memory that a C library allocates would not be counted there, and `maxMemory` would not see it.
- **Windows:** the SDK points the standard output of the process to the error output, as it does on Unix, so `fmt.Println` is harmless. (On Unix the redirection is done on the file descriptor, on Windows on the handle and on `os.Stdout`.) Windows does not let anything overwrite an executable that is running, so on Windows the worker runs from a **copy** (in the temporary folder, named after the time and size of your build) and the file you build stays free: `go build` can replace it while the workers are running, and `fusion.watch('go')` picks the new build up. The copies of old builds are removed. `shadowCopy: true` does the same on any system, `shadowCopy: false` turns it off.

## As a WebAssembly module

The functions of a worker can also be compiled to WebAssembly, which runs in a sandbox without files, network or environment and in one file for every system. It is not a native worker: it runs one call at a time and it is slower. See [WebAssembly](webassembly.md).

## Go, Rust or Python

| | Python | Rust | Go |
|---|---|---|---|
| What it is for | The ecosystem: machine learning, scientific computing, any Python library | Speed, many threads, a small footprint | Network and infrastructure code, many calls at once, easy to build for any system |
| Work per call | Calls overlap in the event loop or in threads, and the GIL limits pure-Python computation | Every call runs in its own thread | Every call runs in its own goroutine |
| Memory of a minimal worker | 24 MB (measured with the components of the tests) | 1 MB (measured with the example worker) | 11 MB (measured with the worker of the tests) |
| What you ship | Your `.py` files, and Python with its libraries on the machine | One binary. The machine does not need Rust | One binary. The machine does not need Go |
| Build for another system | Nothing to build | The target has to be installed, and usually a linker for it | `GOOS` and `GOARCH`, nothing else |
| Change it while the app runs | Save the file | Build again: `fusion.watch('rust')` | Build again (`go build`): `fusion.watch('go')` replaces the workers |
| Contracts | `@action(...)` | `.summary().input().output()...` in code | `.Summary().Input().Output()...` in code |

They can be used in the same application: each runtime has its own pool, and `fusion.python(...)`, `fusion.rust(...)` and `fusion.go(...)` are independent.

## The API of the module

The whole API, with every method, is in [go/README.md](../go/README.md). In short:

- `totalfusion.New().Function(name, func(call *Call) (any, error))` registers a function that answers once, and `.Stream(name, func(call *Call) error)` one that sends chunks with `call.Emit(value)`, which returns an error when the consumer is gone: return it and the stream ends.
- `call.Args` is the argument as a `Value`; `call.Args.Get("key")` never panics, and `.AsString()`, `.AsFloat()`, `.AsInt()`, `.AsBytes()`, `.AsFloat32s()`... tell you whether the value is what you expected.
- `totalfusion.Invalid("...")` is a mistake of the caller (Total.js sends its message to the client); any other error (`totalfusion.NewError("...")` or a plain Go `error`) is a failure that stays in the log. `totalfusion.Named("DatabaseError", "...").WithCode("E_DB")` gives the error a name and a code of its own.
- `.OnShutdown(func() { ... })` runs when the worker is asked to stop. What you do in `main` before `Run()` happens before the worker says it is ready.
- The metadata methods apply to the function registered just before them: `Summary`, `Input`, `Output`, `Query`, `Params`, `Permissions`, `User`, `SA`, `SU`, `Idempotent`, `Timeout`, `ID`, `MCP` and `Action`.

---

<!-- The Go module: go/README.md -->

# totalfusion (Go)

Write functions in Go and call them from Node.js and Total.js as `async` functions. This module is the Go side of [TotalFusion](../README.md): your program registers its functions and TotalFusion starts it, keeps a pool of workers, and talks to it through the standard input and output.

A worker is a normal binary and an **isolated process**: a panic fails only the call that caused it, and even a crash of the whole process never takes Node.js down. Nothing is compiled by TotalFusion: you build the worker (`go build`) or you get it precompiled.

```go
package main

import (
	"unicode/utf8"

	totalfusion "github.com/totaljs-es/totalfusion/go"
)

func main() {
	app := totalfusion.New()

	app.Function("text.length", func(call *totalfusion.Call) (any, error) {
		text, ok := call.Args.Get("text").AsString()
		if !ok {
			return nil, totalfusion.Invalid("text must be a string")
		}
		return map[string]any{"length": utf8.RuneCountInString(text)}, nil
	}).Summary("Counts the characters of a text").Input("*text:String").Output("length:Number").MCP(true)

	app.Run()
}
```

```js
fusion.configure({ go: { binary: './worker/worker', workers: 4 } });

await fusion.go('text.length', { text: 'Hello' });   // { length: 5 }
```

The import path has a `go` at its end and the package is called `totalfusion`, so import it with that name, as above.

## Installing the module

The module is not on a registry: the npm package ships its sources, and the `go.mod` of your worker points to them.

```
module worker

go 1.21

require github.com/totaljs-es/totalfusion/go v0.0.0

replace github.com/totaljs-es/totalfusion/go => ../node_modules/totalfusion/go
```

It needs Go 1.21 or newer and has no dependencies at all (only the standard library, and no `cgo`).

## Functions

- `app.Function(name, func(call *Call) (any, error))` answers once.
- `app.Stream(name, func(call *Call) error)` sends many chunks with `call.Emit(value)`. In JavaScript: `for await (const chunk of fusion.go.stream(name, args))`. `Emit` waits when the consumer is slow (backpressure) and returns `ErrCancelled` when it stops reading, so `if err := call.Emit(x); err != nil { return err }` ends the stream.
- `call.Args` is a `Value`. `call.Args.Get("key")` never panics: a missing member is null.
- `call.Context()` is a `context.Context` that is cancelled when Node.js gave up (timeout, abort) or the worker is asked to stop. Pass it to what the function calls. `call.Cancelled()` is the same as a boolean. A function that never looks is killed after `cancelGrace` and the worker is replaced.
- `app.OnShutdown(func() { ... })` runs when the worker is asked to stop. What you do in `main` before `Run()` (load a model, open a connection) happens before the worker says it is ready.
- Every call runs in its own goroutine, so a function must be safe to run at the same time as itself when `concurrency` is more than 1.

## Values

`Value` holds everything JSON can, plus binary data that never goes through JSON. A function receives it as `call.Args`:

| JavaScript | Go (what you read) |
|---|---|
| string, boolean, `null` | `AsString()`, `AsBool()`, `IsNull()` |
| number | `AsFloat()` for any number, `AsInt()` for an integer (or a float with no decimals) |
| array, object | `At(i)`, `Get(key)`, `AsArray()`, `AsObject()` |
| `Buffer`, `Uint8Array`, `ArrayBuffer` | `AsBytes()` (`[]byte`) |
| `Float32Array`, `Float64Array`, `Int32Array` | `AsFloat32s()`, `AsFloat64s()`, `AsInt32s()` |
| `Int8Array`, `Int16Array`, `Uint16Array`, `Uint32Array`, `BigInt64Array`, `BigUint64Array` | `Raw()`, as `[]int8`, `[]int16`, `[]uint16`, `[]uint32`, `[]int64`, `[]uint64` |

Each `As` method returns the value and whether it was of that type. `Raw()` is the plain Go value (`nil`, `bool`, `int64`, `float64`, `string`, `[]any`, `map[string]any`, or a slice).

A function returns plain Go values: `nil`, booleans, any integer or float, strings, `[]any`, `map[string]any`, and the slices `[]byte` (a `Buffer`), `[]int8`, `[]int16`, `[]uint16`, `[]int32`, `[]uint32`, `[]int64`, `[]uint64`, `[]float32` (a `Float32Array`) and `[]float64`, which travel as raw bytes. Anything else (a struct with `json` tags, a `[]string`, a `map[string]int`) goes through `encoding/json`, which cannot carry binary data. `call.Args.Raw()` can be returned as it is, to echo what arrived.

NaN and infinity cannot be sent (JSON has no such numbers): the call fails with `NOT_SERIALIZABLE`.

## Errors

`totalfusion.NewError("...")` (or a plain Go `error`) is a failure of the function. `totalfusion.Invalid("...")` is a mistake of the caller (bad input): in Total.js its message is sent to the client, and the message of any other error stays in the log. `totalfusion.Named("DatabaseError", "...").WithCode("E_DB")` gives the error a name and a code of its own; it is found even when it is wrapped (`fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)`). A panic becomes an error named `Panic`, and its stack goes to the error output. `Invalidf` and `Errorf` take a format.

## Total.js

The methods that describe a function apply to the function registered just before them: `Summary`, `Input`, `Output`, `Query`, `Params` (the schema syntax of Total.js, `*` means required), `Permissions`, `User`, `SA`, `SU`, `Timeout` (a `time.Duration`), `Idempotent` (the call may be repeated on another worker if this one dies), `ID` and `MCP`. A function that declares any of them, or calls `.Action()`, becomes an action of Total.js with `fusion.register({ runtime: 'go', go: { binary } })`; the others stay callable from JavaScript but private. `MCP(true)` also exposes it to AI agents.

`./worker --describe` prints the contracts as JSON. This is what `register()` and `fusion.doctor('go')` read: no function is called to learn them, but the program starts, so what your `main` does before `Run()` (loading a model, opening a connection) runs too.

## Do not print to the standard output

It carries the protocol. On Unix and on Windows the module redirects it to the error output for you, so `fmt.Println` is harmless, but use `fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, ...)` or the `log` package to be safe everywhere.

## Memory

`totalfusion.Memory()` is the memory of the process in bytes, and whether the system tells it. Every answer carries it, and it is what `maxMemory` looks at. Linux: resident set size. Windows: the private bytes of the process. Other systems, macOS included: the memory that the Go runtime holds, because asking for the footprint needs `cgo`.

## As a WebAssembly module

The same functions can run in the sandbox of [WebAssembly](../docs/webassembly.md): no files, no network, no environment. Call `app.Wasm()` in an `init` function (a module of this kind does not run `main`), build with Go 1.24 or newer, and call it with `fusion.wasm(...)`:

```go
func init() {
	app := totalfusion.New()
	app.Function("math.add", add).Input("*a:Number\n*b:Number")
	app.Wasm()
}

func main() {}
```

```bash
GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -buildmode=c-shared -o module.wasm
```

A module answers once per call: `Emit` returns an error, and a function registered with `app.Stream` is refused. Nothing changes in the code of the other functions.

## Building for another system

```bash
GOOS=linux   GOARCH=amd64 go build -o worker-linux .
GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build -o worker.exe .
GOOS=darwin  GOARCH=arm64 go build -o worker-mac .
```

The module needs no `cgo` and no other tool, so this works from any system.

## Rebuilding while the application runs

Windows does not let anything overwrite an executable that is running, so on Windows TotalFusion runs your worker from a copy and the file `go build` writes stays free (`shadowCopy`, on by default there). With `fusion.watch('go')` the workers are replaced by the new build.

## Requirements

Go 1.21 or newer. Standard library only. Tested with Go 1.21 and 1.27 on macOS (Apple silicon), and in the continuous integration on Linux, macOS and Windows.
